subsection: 4. Sustainable development as a model for the future

notes.b: Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs (Brundtland, 1987).
points: It has three pillars, environmental, economic and social, which must be balanced against each other.
It contrasts with growth-only models that measure development by rising output (see the note “Views of development and underdevelopment”).
“The Limits to Growth” (1972), a report for the Club of Rome, used computer models to warn that unchecked population and economic growth would exhaust resources within about a century.
The Brundtland Report, “Our Common Future”, was produced by the UN World Commission on Environment and Development in 1987.
The Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro (1992) produced Agenda 21 and the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change.
The Millennium Development Goals (eight goals, 2000–2015) were followed by the Sustainable Development Goals: 17 goals adopted in September 2015, with a target year of 2030.
The Paris Agreement (2015) committed countries to tackle climate change.
The world is off track to meet most of the Sustainable Development Goals.

notes.h: Why sustainable development should be a priority
points: Resources are finite and are being overused.
Climate change, biodiversity loss and inequality between and within generations threaten future development.
The poorest people suffer first when resources are degraded.
Growth that destroys the resources it depends on cannot last.

notes.b: The model is widely accepted but hard to apply.
points: It is vague and open to greenwashing, where firms and governments claim sustainability without real change.
The pillars conflict: jobs can be at odds with protecting the environment.
Poorer countries argue that rich countries grew without limits and now ask them to slow down.
The costs of change fall unequally, and progress on the Sustainable Development Goals is behind schedule.

notes.h: Alternative measures for a sustainable future
points: Bhutan’s Gross National Happiness, put forward in the 1970s by King Jigme Singye Wangchuck, measures wellbeing beyond income.
The ecological footprint measures the land and resources a population needs to support its consumption.
Renewable resources should be used no faster than they regenerate, which is the sustainable yield.
Non-renewable resources should be used efficiently and replaced by alternatives where possible.
Reduce, reuse and recycle waste.
Protect biodiversity.
Involve local people in decisions about resources.
Irish fishing has been shaped by past overfishing in EU waters.
The Common Fisheries Policy of 1983 was reformed in 2013, introducing maximum sustainable yield and a landing obligation (a discard ban), phased in during 2015–2019.
The Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority was set up in 2007.
Killybegs, Co. Donegal, is Ireland’s largest fishing port.
The North Sea herring fishery was closed from 1977 to the early 1980s and recovered under quotas.
The Grand Banks cod moratorium of 2 July 1992 cost about 30,000 jobs off Newfoundland and is the warning for overfishing.

notes.b: Bord na Móna has moved from burning peat to renewable energy under its “Brown to Green” strategy.
points: Bord na Móna was founded in 1946.
The Lanesborough and Shannonbridge peat stations closed in December 2020, and peat harvesting ended in January 2021.
Cutaway bogs are being rehabilitated and rewetted, and peatland is valued as a store of carbon.
Lough Boora Discovery Park, Co. Offaly, is one of the rehabilitated sites.
Bellacorick, Co. Mayo, has wind farms on cutaway bog.
Wind provides about a third of Irish electricity, and renewables about two-fifths (early 2020s).
The Climate Action Plan targets 80% renewable electricity by 2030 and at least 5 GW of offshore wind by 2030.
The Climate Act 2021 requires a 51% cut in emissions by 2030 (from 2018) and net zero by 2050.
The East–West Interconnector (2012) links Ireland and Britain, and the Celtic Interconnector to France is due in the late 2020s.
BurrenLIFE (2005–2010) and then the Burren Programme pay farmers according to habitat scores for each field.
Agri-environment schemes have included REPS (1994), GLAS (2015) and ACRES (2023).
Origin Green, Bord Bia’s sustainability programme, began in 2012.
Milk quotas were abolished on 1 April 2015, and the dairy herd grew strongly afterwards.
Agriculture produces over a third of Irish greenhouse gas emissions.
Only about half of Irish waters are in good or high ecological status (EPA, 2016–2021).
Dairy expansion is in tension with water quality and emissions targets.
The plastic bag levy began in March 2002 at 15 cent, and plastic bag use fell by over 90%.
The Deposit Return Scheme (Re-turn) began on 1 February 2024.
Forest cover in Ireland is about 11%, mostly conifer plantations of Sitka spruce.
Coillte was set up in 1988 to manage state forests.
Remnants of native woodland, such as the Killarney oakwoods, show what Ireland has lost.
Ireland needs more native broadleaf woodland.
Managed Scandinavian forests are discussed in the note “An interdependent global economy”.

notes.h: Costa Rica: from deforestation to forest recovery (international case study)
notes.b: Costa Rica, in Central America between Nicaragua and Panama, shows how a country can reverse resource loss.
points: In the 1970s and 1980s forests were cleared for cattle pasture, and by the late 1980s forest covered only about a fifth of the country.
The Payment for Environmental Services programme, started in 1997 and run by the national forestry fund FONAFIFO, pays landowners to protect and replant forest.
The programme is paid for largely by a tax on fuel.
Forest cover has since risen to over half of the country.
About a quarter of the land is in national parks and other protected areas.
Ecotourism is one of the largest sources of foreign income.

notes.h: Costa Rica: renewable energy, defence and spending
points: Since 2015 almost all of Costa Rica’s electricity has come from renewable sources (over 98% in most years, but about 95% in 2023, when drought cut hydropower), mainly hydroelectric, with geothermal and wind.
Costa Rica abolished its army in 1948 and spends instead on education and health.
In 2021 Costa Rica won the first Earthshot Prize (Protect and Restore Nature) for its forest recovery.
Transport still runs mainly on imported oil.
Tourism puts pressure on protected areas.
The Aral Sea: rivers were diverted from the 1960s to irrigate Soviet cotton, and the sea shrank to a fraction of its size; the Kok-Aral dam was built in 2005.
Amazon deforestation, examined in the note “An interdependent global economy”, is another warning of unsustainable use.
Commodity prices are low and unstable, and small farmers receive a tiny share of the final price.
Middlemen take a large share of the value of farmers’ crops.
Poor working conditions and child labour are common in producing countries.
Terms of trade decline as the prices of raw materials fall relative to manufactured goods (see the note “Views of development and underdevelopment”).
Tariff escalation: coffee beans enter rich markets with low tariffs, but roasted, processed coffee faces higher ones.
Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana grow over half of the world’s cocoa, mostly exported as beans.
Fair trade is a trading partnership based on dialogue, transparency and respect that seeks greater equity in international trade.
The first fair trade label, Max Havelaar, was launched in the Netherlands in 1988 for Mexican coffee.
Fairtrade International coordinates the Fairtrade Mark.
Garstang, Lancashire, England, declared itself the world’s first Fairtrade town in 2000.
The Fairtrade Minimum Price is a floor that covers the cost of sustainable production.
The minimum is a floor, not a guaranteed higher price: when the market price is above the minimum, producers receive the market price plus the premium.
The Fairtrade Premium is an extra sum paid to the co-operative, spent on projects the members choose democratically.
Long-term contracts and pre-finance give producers credit before the harvest.
Producers are organised in democratic co-operatives.
Labour standards ban forced and child labour, protect the freedom to join unions and require safe conditions.
Environmental standards restrict pesticides, protect water and forests and ban GM crops.
The Fairtrade Mark is a guarantee to consumers that these standards have been met.
Fairtrade products include coffee, cocoa, tea, bananas, sugar, cotton and flowers.
Close to 2 million farmers and workers belong to Fairtrade-certified producer organisations in about 70 countries.

notes.h: Case study: Kuapa Kokoo and Divine Chocolate, Ghana
notes.b: Kuapa Kokoo is a Fairtrade cocoa farmers’ co-operative in Ghana, the world’s second-largest cocoa producer.
points: Kuapa Kokoo, meaning “good cocoa farmer” in Twi, was founded in 1993.

Divine Chocolate was set up in Britain in 1998, part-owned by Kuapa Kokoo. Since 2020 the German chocolate maker Ludwig Weinrich has held the majority; Kuapa Kokoo kept about 20% of the shares and seats on the board.
Farmers receive a share of Divine’s profits as well as the Fairtrade price and premium.
Premium spending has included wells for clean water, school buildings and mobile health clinics.
Kuapa Kokoo encourages women to take leadership roles in its village societies.
Farmers share in the profits of the brand, not just the beans they sell.

notes.h: Case study: Oromia Coffee Farmers Co-operative Union, Ethiopia
notes.b: The Oromia union in Ethiopia shows how a co-operative can sell directly to buyers.
points: The union was founded in 1999 and led by Tadesse Meskela.
It sells members’ coffee directly to buyers, including Fairtrade coffee, cutting out middlemen.
Its premium has paid for schools, clinics and water.
Its story is told in the documentary “Black Gold” (2006).
Ethiopia is the original home of arabica coffee.

notes.h: Potential impact of fair trade on development
notes.b: Fair trade can contribute to development by changing the position of producers in trade.
points: Higher and more stable income gives farmers money to invest and plan.
The premium funds community projects such as education, health and clean water.
Democratic co-operatives empower producers to take decisions together.
Women’s participation in co-operatives gives women a voice and income.
Organic farming and reduced clearing of land help environmental sustainability.
Child labour can be reduced when families earn a fairer income.
Producers learn processing and marketing skills.
Fair trade raises consumer awareness in rich countries and pressures large firms to change.
Fairtrade Ireland licenses the Fairtrade Mark in Ireland.
Clonakilty, Co. Cork, became Ireland’s first Fairtrade town in 2003.
Towns, schools and universities can apply for Fairtrade status.
Fairtrade Fortnight takes place each year in late February and March.
Supermarkets stock Fairtrade ranges, and Irish NGOs promote fair trade.

notes.h: Limits and criticisms of fair trade
points: Fair trade is only a tiny share of world trade.
Higher prices put off some consumers.
Certification costs exclude the poorest farmers.

A 2014 study by the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS), University of London, of Ethiopia and Uganda found that hired labourers on some Fairtrade-certified farms were paid less than those on comparable non-certified farms; Fairtrade disputed parts of the findings.
Benefits go mainly to co-operative members rather than hired labourers.
Market prices sometimes exceed the minimum price, so the floor then gives no extra protection.
Fair trade does not change the trade rules, such as subsidies and tariff escalation.
Cadbury Dairy Milk carried the Fairtrade Mark from 2009 and switched in 2017 to Mondelēz’s own Cocoa Life scheme in Britain and Ireland (also covered in the note “An interdependent global economy”).
Most value is still added in rich countries unless producers process their own crops, which Divine Chocolate does.

notes.b: Fair trade is a model of sustainable, just trade that improves the lives of those involved and shows what is possible.
points: Its impact on development depends on its scale and on wider changes in trade rules.
Development is not sustainable if it excludes or harms groups of people.
Minority groups often lack political power, so their land and rights are taken for development projects such as dams, mines, plantations and wind farms.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted on 10 December 1948.
ILO Indigenous and Tribal Peoples Convention (No. 169) was adopted in 1989.
The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples was adopted by the UN General Assembly on 13 September 2007; it includes free, prior and informed consent.

notes.h: Indigenous peoples of the Amazon (developing-world case)
points: Indigenous peoples have lost land to ranching, soya, logging, mining and dams.
Brazil’s Census 2022 counted about 1.7 million indigenous people, under 1% of the population.
In 2023 the Brazilian government declared a public health emergency in Yanomami territory after illegal gold mining caused malnutrition and disease.
The Belo Monte dam on the Xingu River, completed in 2019, was opposed by the Kayapó and displaced thousands of people.
Indigenous territories are among the best-protected forests, linking justice to sustainable resource use.
Chico Mendes, a rubber tapper, was murdered on 22 December 1988 at Xapuri, Acre.
Extractive reserves, where forest is harvested sustainably, were set up after his death.

notes.b: Irish Travellers are an ethnic group, not a race. Their case shows how inequality and discrimination block sustainable development for a minority.
points: Irish Travellers were formally recognised as an ethnic minority on 1 March 2017.
The 2022 Census counted about 33,000 Travellers, under 1% of the population.
The All Ireland Traveller Health Study (2010) found that Traveller men lived about 15 years less than men in the general population, and Traveller women about 11.5 years less.
The same study found that the suicide rate among Traveller men was about six times the general rate.
The 2016 Census found that about 80% of Travellers in the labour force were unemployed.
Accommodation shortages persist, and local authority Traveller accommodation budgets have gone unspent.
Discrimination in services is outlawed by the Equal Status Acts (2000).
Responses include equality law, ethnic status and the National Traveller and Roma Inclusion Strategy 2017–2021.
The Roma are Europe’s largest ethnic minority, about 10–12 million people (Council of Europe estimate), many in Romania, Bulgaria, Hungary, Slovakia and Spain.
The Roma face poverty, segregated housing and schools, and discrimination; they were persecuted in the Holocaust.

In D.H. and Others v Czech Republic (European Court of Human Rights, 2007) the court ruled that placing Roma children in “special schools” for children with learning disabilities was unlawful discrimination.
EU frameworks include the Framework for National Roma Integration Strategies (2011) and the Roma strategic framework for equality, inclusion and participation (2020–2030).

notes.h: The Sámi and the Fosen wind farm
notes.b: The Fosen case shows that green development must also be just.
points: The Sámi are the indigenous people of northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia’s Kola Peninsula; reindeer herding is central to their culture.
Fosen, in central Norway, is one of Europe’s largest onshore wind farms.
On 11 October 2021 Norway’s Supreme Court ruled that the turbines, built on reindeer grazing land, violated the herders’ right to enjoy their culture.
The turbines were not removed and kept running after the ruling.
In 2023 Sámi activists, joined by Greta Thunberg, blocked government buildings in Oslo in protest.
In 2023–24 the herders reached agreements with the state and the wind-farm owners.
The Rohingya and Uyghurs are discussed in the note “An interdependent global economy”.
Aboriginal Australians are discussed in the note “Racial groupings”.
Self-reliance means communities and countries meet their own needs with their own resources, skills and decisions.
It reduces dependence on aid, loans, foreign companies and imports, and links to bottom-up development and appropriate technology.

notes.b: Tanzania under Julius Nyerere, its first president, is a mixed example: strong social gains, but economic failure.
points: Tanganyika gained independence in 1961 and united with Zanzibar as Tanzania in 1964.
The Arusha Declaration of 1967 set out socialism and self-reliance, known as Ujamaa.
Ujamaa (“familyhood”) villages and collective farming were created, with education for self-reliance.
Kiswahili was promoted as a uniting national language, and national unity and peace were achieved.
Literacy and school enrolment rose.
Villagisation from 1973 to 1976 moved millions of people, often by force, into planned villages.
Food and export output fell, and the economy went into crisis.
Nyerere stepped down as president in 1985, and in 1986 Tanzania agreed an IMF programme and began market reforms.
Evaluation: Ujamaa gave social gains but was not an economic success, and forced villagisation damaged the model.
Mahatma Gandhi promoted swadeshi (buy Indian) and khadi (hand-spun cloth) as self-reliance against colonial dependence.
Intermediate or appropriate technology is cheap, local and repairable (see the note “Views of development and underdevelopment”).
E. F. Schumacher’s “Small Is Beautiful” (1973) promoted it.
The Intermediate Technology Development Group, founded in 1966, is now Practical Action.
The Green Belt Movement was founded in Kenya in 1977 by Wangari Maathai, and women’s groups have planted tens of millions of trees for fuel, soil and income.
Maathai won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2004, the first African woman to do so.
Zaï pits and stone lines, as used by Yacouba Sawadogo in Yatenga, Burkina Faso, restore degraded farmland.
Farmer-managed natural regeneration in Niger has regreened about 5 million hectares since the 1980s (see the note “Human interference with soils”).
La Via Campesina, an international peasant farmers’ movement founded in 1993, campaigns for food sovereignty, the right of people to control their own food systems.
Grameen Bank, SEWA and co-operatives show self-help through finance (see the note “Empowering people: linking economic growth with human development”).
Muintir na Tíre, a community development movement, was founded in 1937 by Fr John Hayes in Co. Tipperary.
Co-operative creameries and credit unions show self-help in Ireland (see the note “Empowering people: linking economic growth with human development”).
LEADER and community development support local groups in Ireland.
NGOs that help people help themselves include Self Help Africa and Bóthar.
Self-reliance builds dignity, skills and local ownership, and avoids debt and dependency.
Complete self-reliance cuts countries off from trade, investment and technology, as Tanzania showed.
Communities still need fair trade rules, infrastructure and some outside support.

keyTerms.definition: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
The rate at which a renewable resource can be harvested without running it down, because it regenerates at least as fast.
Claiming to be sustainable without making real changes.
The land and resources a population needs to support its consumption.
The rule that fishers must land the fish they catch rather than discard them, introduced in the 2013 reform of the Common Fisheries Policy.
A trading partnership that seeks greater equity in international trade by paying producers fairly and giving them a voice.
A floor price that covers the cost of sustainable production.
An extra sum paid to a co-operative on top of the price, spent on projects the members choose democratically.
Higher import tariffs on processed goods than on raw materials, which discourages producers from processing their own crops.
The right of indigenous peoples to agree or refuse to projects on their land before they go ahead.
Meeting a community’s or country’s own needs with its own resources, skills and decisions.
Julius Nyerere’s model of socialism and self-reliance in Tanzania, based on villages and collective farming.
Cheap, local and repairable technology suited to the needs and resources of a community.
Small planting pits dug in degraded land to trap water and organic matter, used in Burkina Faso.
The right of people to control their own food systems.
A protected area in which forest is harvested sustainably by the people who live in it.

factCards.term: Sustainable development: how the idea developed, in order
factCards.definition: The Limits to Growth (1972, Club of Rome) warned growth would exhaust resources within about a century; Brundtland's Our Common Future (1987); the Rio Earth Summit (1992) and Agenda 21; the MDGs (2000–2015); the 17 SDGs and the Paris Agreement (2015).

factCards.term: Sustainable development: the three pillars and why it is a priority
factCards.definition: Environmental, economic and social pillars must be balanced. It is a priority because resources are finite and overused; climate change and biodiversity loss threaten the future; the poorest suffer first; growth that destroys resources cannot last.

factCards.term: Sustainable development: four problems with the model
factCards.definition: It is vague and open to greenwashing; its pillars conflict, as when jobs clash with protecting the environment; poorer countries argue that rich ones grew without limits and now ask them to slow down; progress on the SDGs is off track.

factCards.term: Irish peatlands: Bord na Móna's shift from brown to green
factCards.definition: Bord na Móna (1946) ended peat harvesting in January 2021, after the Lanesborough and Shannonbridge peat-burning power stations closed in December 2020. Cutaway bogs are rewetted to store carbon, as at Lough Boora, Co. Offaly; Bellacorick, Co. Mayo, has wind farms.

factCards.term: Irish renewable energy: current share and targets
factCards.definition: Wind gives about a third of Irish electricity, renewables about two-fifths (early 2020s). 2030 targets: 80% renewable electricity, at least 5 GW offshore wind, a 51% emissions cut; net zero by 2050. East–West Interconnector (2012); Celtic Interconnector due.

factCards.term: Sustainable farming in Ireland: schemes and the dairy tension
factCards.definition: BurrenLIFE (2005–2010) led to the Burren Programme, paying farmers by habitat scores; REPS (1994), GLAS (2015), ACRES (2023); Origin Green (2012). But dairy grew strongly after quotas ended in 2015; only about half of Irish waters are in good or high status.

factCards.term: Irish waste and forestry: two successes and one gap
factCards.definition: The plastic bag levy (March 2002, 15 cent) cut bag use by over 90%; the Deposit Return Scheme began on 1 February 2024. Forest cover is only about 11%, mostly Sitka spruce (Coillte, 1988); more native broadleaf woodland, like the Killarney oakwoods, is needed.

factCards.term: Costa Rica: how it reversed deforestation
factCards.definition: Clearing for cattle pasture in the 1970s–80s cut forest to about a fifth of the land. The Payment for Environmental Services programme (1997, FONAFIFO), funded largely by a fuel tax, pays landowners to protect and replant; forest now covers over half.

factCards.term: Costa Rica: energy, spending choices, recognition and limits
factCards.definition: Almost all electricity renewable since 2015 (mainly hydro, plus geothermal and wind); ecotourism a top earner; army abolished in 1948, its budget going to education and health; first Earthshot Prize (2021). Limits: transport runs on imported oil; tourism pressure.

factCards.term: The problem fair trade addresses: five features of unfair trade
factCards.definition: Low, unstable commodity prices; small farmers' tiny share of the final price; middlemen taking much of the value; poor conditions and child labour; tariff escalation, as when coffee beans face low tariffs but roasted coffee faces higher ones.

factCards.term: How fair trade works: six features
factCards.definition: A minimum price covering sustainable production (or market price plus premium if higher); a premium spent on projects members choose; long-term contracts and pre-harvest credit; democratic co-ops; no forced or child labour; restricted pesticides, no GM crops.

factCards.term: Fair trade: origins, scale and products
factCards.definition: Max Havelaar, the first label, began in the Netherlands in 1988 for Mexican coffee; Garstang, England, was the first Fairtrade town (2000). Close to 2 million farmers and workers in about 70 countries are certified, growing coffee, cocoa, tea and bananas.

factCards.term: Kuapa Kokoo and Divine Chocolate, Ghana: key facts
factCards.definition: A Fairtrade cocoa co-operative founded in 1993 (good cocoa farmer in Twi). It is a part-owner of Divine Chocolate (Britain, 1998), so farmers share brand profits as well as the Fairtrade price and premium. The premium paid for wells, schools and mobile clinics; women are urged to lead.

factCards.term: Oromia Coffee Farmers Co-operative Union, Ethiopia: key facts
factCards.definition: Founded in 1999 and led by Tadesse Meskela, it sells members' coffee directly to buyers, cutting out middlemen; its premium paid for schools, clinics and water. Its story is told in the film Black Gold (2006). Ethiopia is arabica coffee's original home.

factCards.term: Fair trade's potential impact on development: eight points
factCards.definition: Higher, steadier income to invest; premium-funded schools, clinics and water; democratic co-ops empower members; women gain voice and income; organic farming and less clearing; less child labour; processing and marketing skills; consumer pressure on big firms.

factCards.term: Fair trade in Ireland: named examples
factCards.definition: Fairtrade Ireland licenses the Fairtrade Mark; Clonakilty, Co. Cork, became Ireland's first Fairtrade town in 2003; towns, schools and universities can apply for Fairtrade status; Fairtrade Fortnight runs in late February and March; supermarkets stock ranges.

factCards.term: Fair trade: limits and the SOAS criticism
factCards.definition: Limits: tiny share of world trade; higher prices deter some buyers; certification costs exclude the poorest; trade rules unchanged; value added in rich countries. SOAS (2014): some hired labourers on certified farms in Ethiopia and Uganda earned less than on similar uncertified ones (disputed).

factCards.term: Amazon indigenous peoples: land loss and two justice cases
factCards.definition: Indigenous peoples have lost Amazon land to ranching, soya, mining and dams (Brazil has about 1.7 million indigenous people, Census 2022). Brazil declared a Yanomami health emergency in 2023 over illegal gold mining; the Belo Monte dam (2019), opposed by the Kayapó, displaced thousands.

factCards.term: Irish Travellers: recognition, inequality figures and responses
factCards.definition: About 33,000 (2022), formally recognised as an ethnic minority in 2017. AITHS (2010): men live about 15 years less, women 11.5; male suicide about six times the general rate. About 80% in the labour force unemployed (2016). Responses: Equal Status Acts (2000); Traveller and Roma Inclusion Strategy.

factCards.term: The Roma: size, problems and legal responses
factCards.definition: Europe's largest ethnic minority, about 10–12 million, many in Romania, Bulgaria, Hungary, Slovakia and Spain; poverty and segregated schools. D.H. v Czech Republic (2007) ruled their placement in special schools unlawful. EU frameworks: 2011, 2020–2030.

factCards.term: The Sámi and the Fosen wind farm: green but unjust?
factCards.definition: On 11 October 2021 Norway's Supreme Court ruled that Fosen turbines on reindeer grazing land violated Sámi herders' right to their culture. They kept running, so in 2023 activists, with Greta Thunberg, blocked buildings in Oslo; agreements followed in 2023–24.

factCards.term: Nyerere's Tanzania: what self-reliance achieved
factCards.definition: Tanganyika (independent 1961) joined Zanzibar as Tanzania in 1964. The Arusha Declaration (1967) set out Ujamaa: villages, collective farming, education for self-reliance. Gains: Kiswahili as national language, unity, peace, more literacy and schooling.

factCards.term: Nyerere's Tanzania: where self-reliance failed
factCards.definition: Villagisation in 1973–76 moved millions, often by force, into planned villages; food and export output fell and the economy went into crisis. Nyerere stepped down in 1985 and in 1986 Tanzania agreed an IMF programme: social gains, economic failure.

factCards.term: Community self-help: three African examples and a global movement
factCards.definition: The Green Belt Movement (Kenya, 1977, Wangari Maathai, Nobel Peace Prize 2004): women planting tens of millions of trees; zaï pits (Yacouba Sawadogo, Burkina Faso); farmer-managed regreening of about 5 million hectares in Niger; La Via Campesina (1993).

factCards.term: Irish self-help: four examples
factCards.definition: Muintir na Tíre, founded in 1937 by Fr John Hayes in Co. Tipperary; co-operative creameries (from 1889) and credit unions (from 1958); LEADER (from 1991); NGOs that help people help themselves, such as Self Help Africa (1984) and Bóthar (1991).

questions.prompt: Examine the contribution that fair trade can make to sustainable development.
questions.model: The problem: low and unstable prices, middlemen, poor working conditions and child labour, and declining terms of trade, with tariff escalation on processed goods. How fair trade works: the Fairtrade Minimum Price as a floor, the Fairtrade Premium spent on projects chosen by members, pre-finance and long-term contracts, democratic co-operatives, labour and environmental standards, and the Fairtrade Mark. Case studies: Kuapa Kokoo and Divine Chocolate in Ghana, with the farmers part-owning the brand, the premium spent on wells, schools and clinics, and women in leadership; the Oromia union in Ethiopia, selling directly to buyers. Impact on development: stable income, investment, community projects, co-operative empowerment, women’s participation, environmental gains, less child labour, skills and consumer pressure. Fair trade in Ireland: Clonakilty, Fairtrade Fortnight, and retail ranges. Limits and evaluation: a tiny share of trade, costs that exclude the poorest, the 2014 SOAS findings on hired labourers, benefits limited to members, no change to trade rules, and brands leaving for their own schemes. Conclusion: fair trade is a model of just trade that improves lives, but its impact depends on scale and wider trade reform.

questions.prompt: Sustainability is a model for future human and economic development. Discuss with reference to resource use, justice issues and self-reliance.
questions.model: Resource use: Irish fisheries (the Common Fisheries Policy reform, the Grand Banks warning), the peatland shift and “Brown to Green”, the Burren Programme and agri-environment schemes, and Costa Rica’s forest recovery and renewable electricity, with its limits. Justice issues: the Irish Travellers, with life expectancy and unemployment figures and the Equal Status Acts; the Sámi and the Fosen ruling of 2021; or Amazon indigenous peoples, with the Yanomami emergency and the Belo Monte dam. Self-reliance: Nyerere’s Tanzania, with Ujamaa, villagisation and the 1986 IMF programme; the Green Belt Movement and Wangari Maathai; farmer-managed regeneration in Niger; Irish community self-help through Muintir na Tíre. Evaluation: sustainability offers a model for the future, but each aspect shows that it must be just and must include local people, and self-reliance must still link to trade and technology.

questions.prompt: Sustainable development should be a priority for human and economic development. Discuss.
questions.model: Definition and history: the Brundtland definition of 1987, from “The Limits to Growth” (1972) through the Rio Earth Summit (1992) and the Millennium Development Goals to the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (2015–2030) and the Paris Agreement (2015). Why it is a priority: finite resources and overuse, climate change, biodiversity loss, inequality, and the poorest suffering first. Examples of success: Costa Rica’s forest recovery and renewable electricity, the Irish peatland transition, the Burren Programme and fair trade. Problems and conflicts: greenwashing, conflicting pillars, the Fosen wind farm, and dairy expansion after the end of milk quotas in 2015. Alternatives: Bhutan’s Gross National Happiness and the ecological footprint. Evaluation: the model gives a common goal, but it is vague and off track, so it must be applied with justice and local participation to work for both human and economic development.
